name: Medical-device commercialization
title: Who has time for a faster test?
deck: A commercialization project with a medical-device company, and the clinic workflows that complicated the pitch.
role: Commercialization project team · customer discovery and market analysis
short: We evaluated a point-of-care diagnostic combining rolling circle amplification with an acoustic sensor. The team explored STI testing and emergency infection applications. The most useful discovery was that an assay's runtime and a clinic's time to act are different measurements.
contribution: I participated in the Berkeley commercialization team. This account draws on the team's company meeting, stakeholder interviews, technical analysis and final recommendation.
result: The final presentation recommended exploring emergency bacterial infections. It did not establish an easier regulatory route, a completed market pivot or a clinical performance result.
takeaway: A diagnostic's advantage depends on the work around the instrument: preparing the sample, running the test, handling volume and acting on the result.

sections.title: The appeal of a faster answer
body: The company’s proposed platform paired isothermal rolling circle amplification with acoustic sensing in a cartridge-based system. The presentations emphasized portability, multiplexing and results in roughly 30–35 minutes. Those were product claims in the project materials, not performance measurements generated by our team.

The company meeting moved quickly into details that matter outside a demonstration: which sample goes into each panel, how it is prepared, who operates the instrument and how results enter the clinic's systems. The notes describe different specimens for different applications, including urine or swabs for an STI panel and blood for a tropical-fever panel.

sections.title: The appointment does not pause for the assay
body: The final presentation's workflow analysis identified a practical problem: fitting an on-site test into an appointment could require extra staff time or longer clinician availability. Its SWOT also raised limited simultaneous sample capacity. A device can shorten a laboratory wait and still add work inside a clinic.

That makes ‘faster’ an incomplete buying argument. The important comparison includes specimen handling, queueing, instrument occupancy, result review and communication with the patient. The project did not measure those intervals, but it identified why a workflow study would be more informative than another runtime comparison.

sections.title: The disagreement was useful
body: One clinic interview raised questions about whether the system could handle university and dedicated STI-clinic volumes. Another suggested the runtime could accommodate the university clinic's workload. The deck also records access as a bottleneck in STI testing and greater urgency for actionable results in emergency settings.

I would preserve those differences. A clinic with distributed arrivals, a high-volume screening service and an emergency department do not have the same operating problem. To resolve the disagreement, I would ask for arrival patterns, peak demand, hands-on time and available instruments in each setting. That is a proposed follow-up, not data we already collected.

sections.title: The pivot had its own costs
body: Our final recommendation favored exploring emergency bacterial infections. The reasoning was that rapid, actionable information could matter more in those settings than in a mature STI-testing market. But the same deck notes that sepsis would create biomarker and device-complexity challenges, and that different applications bring different requirements.

Looking back, I would make the recommendation conditional. A more urgent clinical need does not establish an easier product. The specimen, analyte, intended use and evidence requirements all need to remain attached to the market comparison. A large market estimate cannot settle those questions.

sections.title: The study I would put before the market-size slide
body: I would compare a few specific care pathways: where patients enter, when a result changes management, who performs the test and what happens during busy periods. The next step would be a small operational comparison against the site's current workflow, with clinical and regulatory expertise defining the boundaries.

The regulatory interview suggested early feedback and a careful search for a relevant comparator. I treat that as advice recorded during discovery, rather than proof of eligibility for a particular pathway. The outcome of the project was a recommendation and a clearer set of questions.

technical.title: Elapsed time is not the same as work saved
technical.body: A faster result may arrive after the decision it was meant to inform, or require staff effort that the existing pathway outsources. I would record assay runtime, staff hands-on time, instrument occupancy and time to clinical action as separate quantities. Improving one does not imply an improvement in the others. The project raised these workflow questions; it did not collect an operational time study.

technical.title: Keep the assay and the sensor separate
technical.body: The sensing platform is only one part of a diagnostic. Target recognition, amplification, sample preparation and interference affect whether a signal is useful. The meeting notes raise the link between rolling circle amplification and the acoustic sensor, along with specimen-specific preparation. A complete assessment would follow that chain instead of treating sensor sensitivity as diagnostic accuracy.

technical.title: The old slides need a careful reading
technical.body: The materials use varying runtime claims and make confident statements about market entry, competitors and regulatory pathways. This case study treats them as the team's contemporary working analysis. It does not repeat those statements as verified current specifications or regulatory guidance.

technical.title: A workflow comparison has to keep the counterfactual
technical.body: I would compare the proposed pathway with what the clinic actually does today, including what happens when the patient leaves before a result. I would record hands-on minutes separately from instrument occupancy and elapsed time. A shorter assay can reduce one delay while shifting work onto a person who is already fully occupied. The comparison also needs the setting: the same instrument may fit a low-volume practice and struggle in a clinic with clustered arrivals.

technical.title: The first market and the first validation study are linked
technical.body: Choosing an application changes the specimens, organisms, comparator tests and clinical actions that matter. Our recommendation to investigate emergency infection use cases therefore introduced a new validation problem. I would now put the required performance evidence beside each proposed market and identify which experiments transfer across settings. The original slides’ regulatory shorthand should not be treated as current guidance.
